name: Yara Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying information systems, which is a mix of programming, databases and some business. I live above my parents' takeaway, Golden Spoon, and from Thursday to Sunday I work the counter and take phone orders. The rest of the week I'm in lectures, and I catch the bus because parking is a joke. My brother is fourteen and he thinks I'm basically a hacker, which I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it matches what I expected, a helpful tool, nothing dramatic. We tried an online ordering system at the takeaway last year and it saved us about an hour a day, and that was it. I'd tell classmates not to bet their whole plan on a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the degree stays useful and I can plan normally. What I still worry about is the takeaway, because Mum and Dad work seventy hours a week and prices for ingredients keep rising. If the shop did badly, my parents' income goes and I'd have to carry more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and keep helping at the shop. I'd look for a summer data job in a local firm and try to get some experience beyond the counter. I'd also help my parents with the books on a spreadsheet, since they still do it on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a little tired. There's a lot of work, but it's familiar work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the takeaway is a worry. What's the sore spot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cooking oil and rent. Our landlord put the rent up 8 percent last spring, and my parents didn't put prices up much. If a quiet month came, we'd feel it in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that fall on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'd work more shifts and cut my study hours, because someone has to cover the counter. Nobody has said it, but it's understood.

say: It's a helpful **tool** and nothing dramatic, so don't bet your plan on a revolution.
Our ordering system saved about an **hour** a day, and that was it.
think: The degree stays useful, but the **takeaway's** costs keep rising.
If the shop did badly, I'd have to **carry more** for my parents.
do: Look for a summer **data job** with a local firm.
Put my parents' **books** on a spreadsheet instead of paper.
feel: A little **tired**, though the work is familiar.
S0.quote: Our landlord put the rent up 8 percent last spring, and my parents didn't put prices up much.
fieldNote: Her **worry** is the family business and rising costs more than any technology.
An unspoken **duty** to cover the counter shapes her study plans.
She is practical and numbers-minded, in keeping with a **steady** temperament.

steps.text: Look for a summer data job with a local firm
Move the takeaway's books from paper to a spreadsheet
Keep working the counter from Thursday to Sunday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, and the sensible thing is to learn how to use it. I'd tell classmates that writing, checking and coding are exactly what employers want to buy cheaper. I'd also say small businesses like ours will be hit by prices if AI makes big chains cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm in the exposed group. Information systems is screen work: reports, data cleaning, basic code. If firms use AI for those, they'd need fewer juniors, and I'm average on grades. I'd have to be better than my results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools more often and learn them properly, since I only try them now and then. I'd focus on skills AI can't do alone, like talking to customers and understanding a business, which I get from the takeaway. I'd look for a placement year and ask the course tutor how graduates are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit on edge. But I like having a clear thing to work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would AI make big chains cheaper, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, delivery routing, customer service, even menu planning. A chain can cut costs with software, and we can't. Customers would see a lower price and stop coming to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the takeaway use AI in the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. An ordering bot or a simple stock planner, maybe. But Dad doesn't trust it, so I'd have to show him with real numbers first.

say: Employers want **writing, checking and coding** cheaper, so learn how to use the tools.
Small businesses like ours may get squeezed by **chains** using AI.
think: Information systems is **screen work**, so I'm in the exposed group.
I'd have to be better than my **grades** suggest.
do: Use **AI tools** regularly and learn them properly.
Ask the tutor how **graduates** are doing and look for a placement year.
feel: A bit **on edge**, but I like having a clear thing to work on.
S1.quote: A chain can cut costs with software, and we can't. Customers would see a lower price and stop coming to us.
fieldNote: She sees **two threats**: her own entry job and her family's business.
She links her takeaway experience to a **skill** she can sell.
She would need real **numbers** to persuade her dad, which fits her proof-first approach.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant for database coursework every week
Apply for a placement year at a local firm
Show Dad a costed test of an online ordering bot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a clear plan, because two years is not enough for people to adapt. I'd say the same to my parents, who would ask what it means for them. I'd say governments need to step in, but I'd also say it's hard to know what's real until it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared for two reasons. My degree would be a screen-work degree arriving into AGI, and the takeaway would face cheaper rivals. Robots for hands-on work follow around 2031, which includes cooking and delivery. Everything my family relies on could shift together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone and save what I earn at the counter. I'd also talk to my parents about whether to sell the takeaway lease while it still has value. And I'd look for a practical route myself, like an apprenticeship in networks or telecoms, which still needs people on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and hurried. I'm standing in a shop that's about to close, and I don't know which door to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd talk to your parents about selling. How do you think that would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. Mum is proud of the place, and Dad doesn't like talking about money. But if I showed them how the numbers could change, I think they'd listen. They did listen when I showed them the rent problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your own best option in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid route that doesn't depend on grades. An apprenticeship, or a technician job. It's less glamorous than what I planned, but it pays and it's on site.

say: Two years is **not enough** for people to adapt.
Governments need to step in, though it's hard to know what's **real** until it happens.
think: My **degree** and the takeaway could both be hit at the same time.
Robots for hands-on work follow around **2031**, including cooking and delivery.
do: **Cut spending** to the bone and save what I earn at the counter.
Talk to my parents about whether to **sell the lease** while it has value.
feel: **Anxious** and hurried, like standing in a shop about to close with no clear door.
S2.quote: I'm standing in a shop that's about to close, and I don't know which door to use.
fieldNote: Her **family's** livelihood and her own future fall together, which raises the mood sharply.
She would use **numbers** to persuade her parents, as she did over the rent.
Her fallback is **practical**: a paid route that doesn't depend on grades.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only
Show my parents the numbers on selling the lease
Ask about telecoms apprenticeships that need people on site
Save every counter wage into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but gives us a chance, and I'd push to start preparing. I'd tell my parents to keep an eye on costs and to think about the shop's future. I'd say that schools and universities should change what they teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel some pressure. I'd graduate in 2029, with AGI doing thinking work by 2031, and a few years of low demand for juniors. But there's time to build a skill that isn't plain screen work. The takeaway might survive until robots in 2034, and maybe beyond if we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and spend summers in a placement. I'd lean towards the business side, like helping small shops with their systems, because that mixes customers and tech. I'd also put money aside for my parents' retirement, in case the takeaway has to close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Nervous, but also like I can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help small shops with their systems. Would they pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. Local shops don't have a tech person. I did our ordering page myself, and a florist next door asked me to do one too. They hate setting up new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the takeaway has to close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then my parents need a plan. I'd want them to have savings and a pension I can add to. I'd also like them to be able to work fewer hours before they're worn out.

say: Five years is **tight** but gives us a chance to prepare.
Schools and universities need to change what they **teach**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 into a few years of **low demand** for juniors.
The takeaway might last until **2034** if we're careful.
do: Spend summers in **placements** and lean towards business-side tech.
Put money aside for my parents' **retirement** in case the shop closes.
feel: **Mixed**, nervous but also like I can do something about it.
S3.quote: Local shops don't have a tech person. I did our ordering page myself, and a florist next door asked me to do one too.
fieldNote: She has a **proof** of demand: the florist who asked for help.
She **plans** around her parents' retirement, not just her own career.
Time turns the **alarm** of 2028 into a project.

steps.text: Offer ordering pages to local shops like the florist
Take a summer placement after second year
Add to a retirement pot for Mum and Dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people use it properly, and it's the sensible moment to ask what we want. I'd tell classmates not to panic but not to coast either. I'd tell my parents to keep running the shop and think about slowing down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly relaxed. By 2036 I'd be 28, with experience and savings and probably a decent job. The takeaway may have been sold by then, and that's fine. Robots come about 2039, and I'd keep an eye on that, but I'd be settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a business-systems job in a bank or a logistics firm, somewhere that values a mix of tech and people skills. I'd keep helping my parents, and save for a small flat. I'd try more AI tools at work when I see colleagues using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. There's still pressure, but it's the ordinary kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the ordinary pressure in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, my loan and my parents getting older. If they get ill and the shop closes, I'd be paying for things. That is normal for anyone, but it counts for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this one different from the 2031 picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a sprint, and ten is a plan. I'd have a first job and a bit of savings before anything big happened.

say: Ten years is plenty of time, so **don't panic** and don't coast either.
My parents should keep running the shop and think about **slowing down**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with **experience** and savings.
Robots come around **2039**, but I'd be settled by then and still watching closely.
do: Take a **business-systems** job in a bank or logistics firm.
**Save** for a small flat and keep helping my parents.
feel: Quite **calm**, with only the ordinary kind of pressure.
S4.quote: Five years is a sprint, and ten is a plan.
fieldNote: The **ordinary pressure** she names is rent, loans and ageing parents.
A decade moves her from **alarm** to a plan.
She keeps her **parents** in view even when her own path is secure.

steps.text: Take a business-systems job at a bank or logistics firm
Save for a small flat in the first three years
Help my parents plan reduced hours at the takeaway

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my family and my future would both be hit at once. What would help is a clear safety net for small shops, and real advice for people like my parents who've never had a pension. And honest information about which jobs will last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my brother. My brother is fourteen, and he's the one who will grow up inside all this. I'd like to know there's something for him that isn't just a screen.

headlineQuote: My brother is fourteen, and he's the one who will grow up inside all this. I'd like to know there's something for him that isn't just a screen.
portrait: Yara is 18, studies **information systems** and lives above her parents' takeaway, working the counter four days a week.
She is a pragmatic centrist who tries tools once they're proven and wants **numbers** before she acts.
Her mood rests on two things at once: her own first job and her **family's** shop.
With thin money she is uneasy in quiet worlds and **alarmed** if AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because her family and her future are hit together.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **safety net** for small shops and a pension plan for parents like hers.
Honest **information** about which jobs will last.
